content: The timing of introducing complementary feeding (CF) in infants has been studied extensively to evaluate its impact on various health and developmental outcomes. Observational studies have compared the effects of introducing CF before six months of age versus at or after six months among full-term infants. The outcomes assessed include stunting, underweight, wasting, thinness, height-for-age z-scores, weight-for-age z-scores, weight-for-height z-scores, length, weight, body mass index (BMI), BMI z-scores, head circumference, overweight, obesity, combined overweight and obesity, triceps and subscapular skinfold thickness, anemia, iron deficiency anemia, iron deficiency, hemoglobin levels, serum ferritin, atopic dermatitis, asthma, diarrhea, lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI), wheezing, eczema, food allergies, malnutrition, gastrointestinal illnesses, respiratory illnesses, and rickets. Subgroup analyses have also been conducted based on settings and feeding practices. For example, early introduction of CF (<6 months) compared to later introduction (≥6 months) has been evaluated in preterm infants, with outcomes such as underweight and weight-for-age z-scores being assessed. Late introduction of CF (after six months) compared to introduction at or before six months has also been studied, with outcomes including stunting, underweight, wasting, thinness, length, weight, BMI, overweight, obesity, anemia, atopic dermatitis, asthma, wheezing, eczema, LRTI, intestinal helminth infections, diarrhea, and food hypersensitivity. Subgroup analyses by setting and feeding practices have been conducted to further explore these outcomes. For preterm infants, comparisons of CF introduced at three months versus four months have been made, focusing on health problems and population-specific outcomes. Similarly, studies have evaluated the introduction of CF at four months versus six months in low birth weight (LBW) or preterm infants, assessing outcomes such as severe anemia (hemoglobin <100 g/L). The studies referenced in this analysis include randomized controlled trials and observational studies, with varying levels of bias and methodological quality. Some studies have been downgraded in their evidence quality due to small sample sizes, high heterogeneity, unclear risk of bias, or lack of adjustment for confounding factors. These limitations highlight the need for careful interpretation of the findings. In summary, the timing of complementary feeding introduction has significant implications for infant growth, nutritional status, and health outcomes. The evidence suggests that both early and late introduction of CF can have distinct effects, and the optimal timing may vary based on individual and population-level factors. Further high-quality research is needed to provide clearer guidance on the timing of CF introduction for different infant populations. This professional summary captures the essence of the studies and outcomes discussed in the original text while maintaining a clear and concise format.
